items.text:
文｜贺哲馨


编辑｜乔芊


传奇


上个世纪 90 年代，每个美国女人的鞋柜里都有一双 Nine West。


这不是夸张的说法，《纽约时报》1997 年就是这么写的。在女鞋这个品类里，Nine West 是全球产业链分工最早、也最彻底的受益者。在 Zara、H&M、优衣库席卷世界之前，它已经提前二十年践行了这套打法。


1969 年，意大利裔美国人 Vince Camuto 接到了来自日本住友银行的邀约。银行希望分散投资，请他去巴西做自有品牌鞋的设计与进口——那里原料充足、人工便宜、大量工厂空着。多次往返巴西的过程中，Camuto 结识了同为住友银行承包方的 Jerome Fisher。


1977 年 5 月，Fisher Camuto Corporation 在纽约成立。两人自立门户时，对外的说法是一句话：日本的钱、意大利的设计、巴西的制造。


公司成立第一年营收就达到 900 万美元。1978 年搬到纽约西 57 街 9 号，Camuto 说他望向窗外看到数字“九”，品牌名 Nine West 因此而来。


1995 年底的高光时期，Nine West 占据了美国百货渠道女鞋销售的 35%。作为参照，同期 Nike 在美国品牌运动鞋市场是 32%。

Nine West九零年代的广告


1999 年，Nine West 以 19.2 亿美元的年营收被成衣集团 Jones Apparel 收购。此后二十年，北美百货渠道系统性衰退，Zara 等快时尚蚕食份额，而它对消费趋势的变化应对不力。2018 年，Nine West 宣告破产，品牌随后被国际品牌管理公司 Authentic Brands Group（以下称 Authentic）以超过 3.4 亿美元买下，一并买走的还有姐妹品牌 Bandolino。


近五十年后，Authentic 执行副总裁兼大中华区负责人 Josh Perlman 向 36 氪回忆起这个品牌创立的初衷，以及延续至今的价值观：


“Vince Camuto 和 Jerome Fisher 在纽约创立这个品牌，是为了把纽约风格、新的职业生活方式带给女性——所以当她们去参加第一次面试时，看起来和感觉都很好。这确实是这个品牌的基石，未来也将如此。”


我们的对话发生在 9 月 9 日——Nine West 诞生于 2017 年的“9×9”科技，一套宣称让高跟鞋“从早上九点到晚上九点都舒适”的技术，在这一天推出了优化后的新版本。


Authentic 位于上海南京西路的办公室为此重新布置，每一个空间都被装置成 Nine West 不同时期的主题展览。从 42 楼的窗外望去，远处浦东三件套和近处鳞次栉比的高楼，也有了一丝曼哈顿的影子。


把产品重新设计一遍的动作，恰好落在一个微妙的时点上。市场调查公司 Circana 最新的零售追踪数据显示，过去十年引领市场潮流的运动生活方式鞋（sport lifestyle）放缓迹象明显，而那些能够从休闲场合平滑过渡到正式场合的产品——芭蕾鞋、厚底套脚鞋、穆勒鞋——销量有所上升。Circana 判断，下半年这一板块仍有上行空间，而舒适仍然是消费者未来购鞋的首要驱动因素。

Nine West于Authentic办公室的展览


不过，Josh Perlman 明白，即使为高跟鞋打上舒适的标签，要回到当初的巅峰也并不容易。他给 Nine West 定下的目标很实际：消费者的���双鞋里有一双是 Nine West，就很不错了。


“我们的挑战在于：那种真正的高跟、真正得体的职业形象，也许你不会穿太多次。但我们会用这个 DNA 往外扩展，也许我们能拿下你十双鞋里的两三双，这就是很好的结果了。但我们希望你的鞋柜里至少有一双 Nine West。”


要达到这个目标，Authentic 需要在中国找一个伙伴。


打磨


在黄文辉看来，过去五年，Nine West 在中国才刚刚完成品牌的初步建设。


2021 年，黄文辉创立的巨爵集团旗下公司美熙实业接下 Nine West 的中国运营权。这家泉州的零售运营商此前主力在线上，客户大多是本地的国产运动品牌——安踏、特步、德尔惠、贵人鸟。“因为这些品牌是我们泉州鞋服行业的标杆企业。”


起初黄文辉做的是这些品牌的线上经销，没有独家授权。2008 年北京奥运前后，全民运动热潮把品牌的预期抬到高点，紧接着是大量开店、大量库存，然后是线上的大量倾销。中国电商平台也正是在那个节点上起量，缺的正是品牌，双方一拍即合。黄文辉的团队就是在那一轮里长起来的。


但库存总有清完的一天。之后品牌不再有尾货，转而做线上专供，他代理的国内品牌也大多变成了上市集团旗下品牌的线上运营与线上授权。直到2020 年五六月，疫情把一切按了暂停键，不得不重新思考未来。

黄文辉在Nine West“9X9”科技发布的现场


“我们那个时候就开始想，如果有机会能去运作更有价值的品牌。更有价值的品牌得具备几个点：第一，品牌之前得有一定的影响力，不论当年多风光，至少原来有一定的基础；第二，在中国市场也还得有影响力；然后还得能让我们有相当的权限去做产品的开发、渠道的建设。”


Nine West 就是这样进入黄文辉视野的。团队里唯一一个做过女鞋的人告诉他，这个品牌在天猫特别厉害——2011、2012 年的双十一，它一直占着“海景房”的位置。“这个品牌如果能运作，我们团队一定非常有信心。”


历史上，Nine West在内地运营权随着母公司所有权更迭也几经易手。2011年前后，Nine West的内地运营权尚属于香港公司GRI，后者是Nine West当时母公司Jones Apparel的亚洲独家分销商。GRI内地经销权随着2018年Nine West的破产而宣告终结，随之而来的是三年空白期。


等黄文辉真正接手之后，团队要解决的第一个问题是：如何在保持品牌基因的同时，回应当下的舒适化潮流，“中国休闲鞋占比大约是市场的 50% 以上，中国人对休闲鞋类的需求远远大于美国人。”


黄文辉的团队有着产品开发权利，但终审权在纽约。他告诉 36 氪，中方设计团队一年两次向纽约总部寄送实物，此外还有多轮图样往返审核，一些“过于休闲”的鞋款会被否决——不过“整体鞋类的通过率是非常高的”。


Nine West 主力产品的价格在 1000 至 2000 元之间，这是属于线下成交的舒适区间。于是，一个曾经擅长线上经营的团队开始研究门店陈设。


这对他们来说是个新课题：服装的陈列面积天然更大，一件衣服的陈列面可能相当于三双鞋；一旦给了空间，服装就会在有限的零售面积里持续扩张，鞋反而被挤到边上。黄文辉说，他们有部分只卖鞋的门店，店效比鞋服混合的门店还要高。但服装对品牌形象的提升、对连带率和客单价的拉动同样明显，是零售空间里不可或缺的一环。


“我们一直在调整（两者面积的比例），我们最理想的是希望服装占三成、四成，鞋子占六成甚至七成，我觉得这是很理想的一个状态。”


除了混合陈列，门店还需要保持新鲜感。Nine West 不是快时尚品牌，但黄文辉要求货架“每一到两个星期”就有新产品上架，并且尤其留意在旗舰店、形象店里维持全价销售。表现不如意的产品会有 30 天的市场反应期，如果还是不行，就顺次下沉到奥莱、唯品会和拼多多这类平台。


“目前团队的补单率在 50%，未来希望能够达到 60% 甚至 70%。”


Nine West 目前有 20 至 30 家门店，未来会线上线下同步拓展，集中在一二线城市——“重点城市、重点突破，聚焦鞋品类。” 谈及Nine West的扩张思路，黄文辉告诉36氪。


未来


回头看，Nine West 的崛起堪称天时地利人和。


七零年代后，更多职业女性进入办公室，从传统的“家庭采购代理人”转变为拥有独立财政自主权的强大消费者，职业正装和高跟鞋的需求得以爆发性增长。


纸媒和电视把欧洲奢侈品从“少数人的裁缝店”炒作成“全球欲望标签”，而 Nine West 做的，是把这种欲望“翻译”成 50 到 65 美元的商品。巴西的工厂让它有能力做到这一点——从交付设计规格到收到成品只需八周，“从 T 台到卖场”的周期被压缩到一季以内。这些工厂最初每天为 Nine West 生产 200 双鞋，到 1993 年，这个数字是每天 13 万双。


与此同时，战后美国中产阶级移居郊区的浪潮在七八十年代达到顶峰，百货公司正迎来历史上的黄金时期。而 Nine West 是首批提出在百货公司里开展 shop in shop 形式的公司之一，这一形式帮助品牌在省下人力和租金的同时，极大提升了品牌价值。1993 年 2 月上市时，公司已经有 236 家零售与奥莱店，同时向 2000 多家百货、专业店和独立店供货。


半个世纪后，这三个条件在中国的节点上再次成立。年轻一代中国女性进入职场的比例和层级都在抬升，接受高等教育的女性比例已超过男性，超过五成女性在第三产业就业。而婚姻的时间轴整体后移，这让她们从进入职场到组建家庭之间的那段时间比上一代长了好几年，那正是需要正装的年纪。


而中国（准确的说，是福建）的工厂提供了媲美当年巴西的速度。巴西的八周在今天是一到两周，黄文辉的团队一年做四季，几乎每一到两个星期就有新品上架。百丽等女鞋企业大幅关店之后留下了百货档口的空间——从 2017 财年的 2.08 万家门店，收缩到 2023 年 11 月的 8361 家。


而需求本身，在黄文辉看来从未消失：“其实正装的、商务的高跟鞋、鞋靴之类的产品，依然有市场需求，特别是在一些很正式的、包括社交的场合，依然需要一双真的好穿又舒适的高跟鞋。但目前市面上，要做到好穿又舒适、跟高到 7.5 甚至更高的品牌，其实是为数不多的，这也是一个痛点。”

图片来源：NIne Weat


这不只是一个经营者对自己生意的判断。同样的观察已经出现在卖方研究里。


去年，Williams Trading 分析师 Sam Poser 在将同业品牌 Steve Madden 的评级从“持有”上调至“买入”时表示，时装鞋的周期已近，因为“看起来女性打开衣柜，发现自己没有新的正装鞋了”。而在美国市场，这些新的平台鞋和猫跟正装鞋，零售价比过去两年热卖的时尚运动鞋高出 30% 到 70%——意味着更高的单价和更厚的毛利。


2026 年 1 月，由 Laurent Vasilescu 带领的 BNP Paribas 分析师团队在研究报告里写道：运动休闲的大周期正在回归常态，消费者正在转回更正式的品类。这条判断被 SGB Media 概括为“华尔街最新一家喊出正装回归的机构”，依据是零售商在季度财报电话会上的表述，以及谷歌趋势的搜索数据。


也许，女性从未打算放弃高跟鞋，她们放弃的是忍耐。


Nine West 押的就是这条缝隙——九项科技、早九点到晚九点、7.5 公分，说到底都在回答同一个问题：能不能让一双高跟鞋，不再需要被咬牙穿完。

上个世纪 90 年代，每个美国女人的鞋柜里都有一双 Nine West。

1969 年，意大利裔美国人 Vince Camuto 接到了来自日本住友银行的邀约。银行希望分散投资，请他去巴西做自有品牌鞋的设计与进口——那里原料充足、人工便宜、大量工厂空着。多次往返巴西的过程中，Camuto 结识了同为住友银行承包方的 Jerome Fisher。
1977 年 5 月，Fisher Camuto Corporation 在纽约成立。两人自立门户时，对外的说法是一句话：日本的钱、意大利的设计、巴西的制造。

半个世纪后，这三个条件在中国的节点上再次成立。年轻一代中国女性进入职场的比例和层级都在抬升，接受高等教育的女性比例已超过男性，超过五成女性在第三产业就业。而婚姻的时间轴整体后移，这让她们从进入职场到组建家庭之间的那段时间比上一代长了好几年，那正是需要正装的年纪。
而中国（准确的说，是福建）的工厂提供了媲美当年巴西的速度。巴西的八周在今天是一到两周，黄文辉的团队一年做四季，几乎每一到两个星期就有新品上架。百丽等女鞋企业大幅关店之后留下了百货档口的空间——从 2017 财年的 2.08 万家门店，收缩到 2023 年 11 月的 8361 家。
而需求本身，在黄文辉看来从未消失：“其实正装的、商务的高跟鞋、鞋靴之类的产品，依然有市场需求，特别是在一些很正式的、包括社交的场合，依然需要一双真的好穿又舒适的高跟鞋。但目前市面上，要做到好穿又舒适、跟高到 7.5 甚至更高的品牌，其实是为数不多的，这也是一个痛点。”
图片来源：NIne Weat
这不只是一个经营者对自己生意的判断。同样的观察已经出现在卖方研究里。
去年，Williams Trading 分析师 Sam Poser 在将同业品牌 Steve Madden 的评级从“持有”上调至“买入”时表示，时装鞋的周期已近，因为“看起来女性打开衣柜，发现自己没有新的正装鞋了”。而在美国市场，这些新的平台鞋和猫跟正装鞋，零售价比过去两年热卖的时尚运动鞋高出 30% 到 70%——意味着更高的单价和更厚的毛利。
2026 年 1 月，由 Laurent Vasilescu 带领的 BNP Paribas 分析师团队在研究报告里写道：运动休闲的大周期正在回归常态，消费者正在转回更正式的品类。这条判断被 SGB Media 概括为“华尔街最新一家喊出正装回归的机构”，依据是零售商在季度财报电话会上的表述，以及谷歌趋势的搜索数据。
也许，女性从未打算放弃高跟鞋，她们放弃的是忍耐。
Nine West 押的就是这条缝隙——九项科技、早九点到晚九点、7.5 公分，说到底都在回答同一个问题：能不能让一双高跟鞋，不再需要被咬牙穿完。

items.text:
文｜王欣逸


编辑｜张雨忻


如果你近期有和投资人闲聊两句，会得出这样一个结论：AI圈的关注点再一次回到了模型和AI Infra（基础设施）。模型，对应着时下应用遇冷，热度向上游转移；而AI Infra的关注点之一，是后训练平台和推理平台。


昨天，Mind Lab发布了他们的最新成果：推出面向行业的模型后训练与推理平台Mint Recursive，以及基于这一平台做后训练的模型Macaron-V1.1。


Macaron-V1.1是一个基于GLM-5.3做后训练、参数为752B的模型。 7月，Mind Lab创始人陈锴杰告诉我们，从基于GLM-5.1后训练的Macaron-V1-Preview到基于GLM-5.2的Macaron-V1，中间只隔了不到一个月。而迭代还在加速，据了解， Macaron-V1.1从上一代迭代而来仅用了不到两周。


Macaron-V1.1由744B的基座模型和四个2B的LoRA专家模块组成，其中四个LoRA分别负责Chat、Agent、Coding和Generative UI（生成式UI）。


从V1的1B LoRA变成了现在的2B LoRA，他们也正在摸索更为理想的专家参数规模。从Benchmark结果来看，相比V1，V1.1在6个Agent榜单上全面提升，在SWE-Marathon（超长程AI编程能力）表现尤为出色。。

△Macaron-V1.1 benchmark表现，来源：企业


更值得注意的是，Macaron V1.1完全基于Mint Recursive完成训练。


Mint Recursive是一个后训练与推理平台，其工作流程包括测评、数据、后训练与部署推理，用户通过API和Python SDK即可调用平台的训练和部署能力；还能接入生产环境中的反馈，让模型在真实任务中持续改进。而这套流程，Mint Recursive 在Macaron V1.1模型的迭代上已经跑通。


就在这一节点，Mind Lab集中发布了一系列成果，把过去一段时间在持续学习与Infra领域积累的Know-how，沉淀为一套可对外提供的服务。


做后训练的Infra


Mind Lab一边做模型、一边做Infra，这并不让人意外。


在今年1月，他们就率先推出了Mint Recursive的早期形态——一个关于LoRA训推的基础设施平台，为客户提供大模型后训练全流程解决方案。


与此同时，在Infra层面下功夫，正慢慢成为一个行业共识。


几天前，智谱创始人、首席科学家唐杰在X上发了一篇长文，阐述了他们用AI改进AI的最新进展，他们让GLM-5.3驱动的Infra Agent，自动优化GLM-5.3自己的推理引擎，让一个超10万张国产芯片组成的集群，在不到两周的时间里，将端到端吞吐提升至初始基线的3倍。


智谱正在做的就是让AI去自我改进推理层Infra。同样是模型参与优化自己，大家想解决的问题不同——Mind Lab要做一个后训练平台，想优化的是从整个后训练到部署推理的流程，囊括数据、评测、部署、反馈收集等步骤。


Mint Recursive平台由三大模块组成：Train&Deploy（训练与部署）、Env Hub（环境中心）、Data&Experience（数据与经验）。这一平台支持模型、SFT（监督微调）、RL（强化学习）、DPO（偏好训练）、全参微调等算法，兼容GLM、Qwen、DeepSeek、Kimi、MiniMax等多种尺寸的开源模型；训练完成后可一键部署，还有配套的测评体系，为下一轮模型训练做准备。


去年9月，OpenAI前CTO Mira Murati创办的Thinking Machines Lab发布了一篇名为《LoRA Without Regret》的技术博客，从理论和实验上证明了，只要方法得当，LoRA的效果可以比肩全参数微调。从那以后，LoRA几乎成了后训练领域的普遍采用的方案。


值得一提的是，Mind Lab一直关注“LoRA”这一后训练范式，这次他们也在这条路线上更进一步，在Mint Recursive中，他们用LoRA把训练和部署都做成了Serverless（无服务器）的模式：客户无需自己买GPU、管理集群，可以直接按Token用量计费。


在训练侧，Mint Recursive想实现的是让模型更聪明——用LoRA的方式，只训练一些少量的新增参数，根据业务目标，不断从业务反馈中学习、持续迭代能力，让模型变得更懂业务，与此同时，还能显著降低企业后训练的开销。


在部署侧，4个LoRA专家模块对应的4个业务版本各自是一个轻量级的Adapter（外挂插件），挂在同一个基座模型上。这些Adapter互不干扰、非常灵活，每个Adapter都能单独升级、上线与下线，历史版本也保留着，便于客户对照与回滚。客户也可以把某个Adapter合并到基座模型里，变成一个完整的、独立的模型。


这也正是LoRA的核心思路，共用基座模型，在每个业务场景只做针对性的后训练。好处在于，模型后训练、部署与迭代的成本能实现大幅下降，调整权重也更加灵活。


后训练所需的数据、评测、反馈等，每一步都离不开Infra的支撑。从做后训练到做后训练Infra，Mind Lab的选择很自然。


但在交出Mint Recursive答卷之前，他们也能做了很多准备：


2025年，Mind Lab开始在Kimi K2这样的万亿参数模型上做后训练研究，Mint Recursive的基础设施最早也是那时开始搭的；


随后，2025年底，他们向NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge贡献了业界首个1T参数量级的LoRA-RL，为Megatron补充了面向超大规模基座的轻量化强化学习的经验；


2026年中，参与火山引擎的强化学习训练框架veRL、NVDIA的下一代训练后端megatron_lite等多个开源项目，提供了一些LoRA和强化学习解决方案；


2026年7月，Macaron-V1系列正式发布并开源，验证了这套训练方案在Agent、Coding等任务中的有效性。


Infra很重要，但不是所有公司都能做Infra，以及有必要单独做Infra。


万亿模型的后训练，工程难度远超想象。分布式训练的显存调度、训推一致性的精度对齐、异步RL的权重热更新，对于一家创业公司而言，每一块都是硬骨头。


陈锴杰告诉我们，训练小模型的强化学习其实很容易，但是一旦规模上来了，难度会变得非常大，尤其是他们还在强化学习之上，叠加了LoRA的持续学习训练方法。


目前，Mint Recursive主要提供三种服务：类似FDE形式的专家与企业一起完成训练；依托平台进行自动化训练；企业通过API和Python SDK自主训练。


训一个企业自己的模型


越来越多企业想要拥有自己的模型，这也是轻量的后训练、持续学习的训练范式被推崇的原因。


从落地角度看，企业端或许是定制化模型最为迫切的场景。“通用大模型仅能覆盖各行业20%-30%的场景，剩下70%-80%的部分，都需要垂直持续学习来优化。”陈锴杰提到。


海外市场已经先一步验证了这个趋势。Fireworks AI，一家做开源模型推理和后训练托管的硅谷公司，今年7月，其估值已经达到175亿美元，ARR突破10亿美元，日Token处理量超过40万亿。


Fireworks AI CEO乔琳在和红杉的对谈中提到：“后训练已经不是模型团队专属游戏了，AI产品在找到PMF、开始规模化后，后训练几乎是它们绕不开的一门必修课。”


具体来看，相比于模型厂商，AI产品公司的壁垒在于用户真实使用产生的数据、真实任务、反馈与偏好等。Fireworks平台上95%以上的流量，来自客户自己微调的专用模型，而不是通用基座。这一逻辑，被乔琳定义为“拥有自己的智能”。


“应用公司做模型”这一选择，正发生在越来越多的企业身上—— AI应用的竞争点从产品本身，逐渐变成产品的经验智能，包括自己的判断、Taste、业务数据和对客户的理解等方面。


应用公司最独特的资产来自真实生产环境：它知道用户究竟想完成什么、哪些结果算好、哪里反复失败，以及专业人员真正怎样判断结果。如何让企业拥有自己的智能、把行业经验合并进基座模型中？


Mint Recursive在尝试的就是 让企业建立起自己的评测体系、奖励机制、训练数据，把后训练做成一个持续迭代的闭环 ：模型在服务用户后积累下真实任务场景数据，每次交互的轨迹，无论成功还是失败，都会被完整记录下来。


这其中，失败的轨迹相当有价值，哪里做错了、为什么错、应该怎么改，平台在找到问题和解决方法后，这些判断和轨迹会直接变成新的训练数据；用新数据重新训练完上线后，又会产生新的反馈，新的反馈又变成下一轮训练的输入，如此循环往复。


平台中的Env Hub（环境）环节容易被忽略，但它尤其关键。英伟达的一篇Agentic RL技术博客中提到，做Agent强化学习需要环境来定义数据集、验证器和状态。环境不只是模型的训练场，也是评测场，评测、合成数据、强化学习，都可以在一套环境中完成。


尽管Mint Recursive中的Recursive（递归）还处于初级形态——人依然在递归的回路中，离模型全自动自己训练还比较遥远，但模型迭代方向已经很明确了。对客户而言，更为重要的不是模型本身，而是企业手里的一线业务现场与独一无二的真实业务数据。


图片来源｜企业供图

欢迎关注～

欢迎交流～


本文来自微信公众号“智能涌现”，作者：王欣逸，36氪经授权发布。

2025年，Mind Lab开始在Kimi K2这样的万亿参数模型上做后训练研究，Mint Recursive的基础设施最早也是那时开始搭的；
随后，2025年底，他们向NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge贡献了业界首个1T参数量级的LoRA-RL，为Megatron补充了面向超大规模基座的轻量化强化学习的经验；
2026年中，参与火山引擎的强化学习训练框架veRL、NVDIA的下一代训练后端megatron_lite等多个开源项目，提供了一些LoRA和强化学习解决方案；
2026年7月，Macaron-V1系列正式发布并开源，验证了这套训练方案在Agent、Coding等任务中的有效性。
Infra很重要，但不是所有公司都能做Infra，以及有必要单独做Infra。
万亿模型的后训练，工程难度远超想象。分布式训练的显存调度、训推一致性的精度对齐、异步RL的权重热更新，对于一家创业公司而言，每一块都是硬骨头。
陈锴杰告诉我们，训练小模型的强化学习其实很容易，但是一旦规模上来了，难度会变得非常大，尤其是他们还在强化学习之上，叠加了LoRA的持续学习训练方法。
目前，Mint Recursive主要提供三种服务：类似FDE形式的专家与企业一起完成训练；依托平台进行自动化训练；企业通过API和Python SDK自主训练。
训一个企业自己的模型
越来越多企业想要拥有自己的模型，这也是轻量的后训练、持续学习的训练范式被推崇的原因。
从落地角度看，企业端或许是定制化模型最为迫切的场景。“通用大模型仅能覆盖各行业20%-30%的场景，剩下70%-80%的部分，都需要垂直持续学习来优化。”陈锴杰提到。
海外市场已经先一步验证了这个趋势。Fireworks AI，一家做开源模型推理和后训练托管的硅谷公司，今年7月，其估值已经达到175亿美元，ARR突破10亿美元，日Token处理量超过40万亿。
Fireworks AI CEO乔琳在和红杉的对谈中提到：“后训练已经不是模型团队专属游戏了，AI产品在找到PMF、开始规模化后，后训练几乎是它们绕不开的一门必修课。”
具体来看，相比于模型厂商，AI产品公司的壁垒在于用户真实使用产生的数据、真实任务、反馈与偏好等。Fireworks平台上95%以上的流量，来自客户自己微调的专用模型，而不是通用基座。这一逻辑，被乔琳定义为“拥有自己的智能”。
“应用公司做模型”这一选择，正发生在越来越多的企业身上—— AI应用的竞争点从产品本身，逐渐变成产品的经验智能，包括自己的判断、Taste、业务数据和对客户的理解等方面。
应用公司最独特的资产来自真实生产环境：它知道用户究竟想完成什么、哪些结果算好、哪里反复失败，以及专业人员真正怎样判断结果。如何让企业拥有自己的智能、把行业经验合并进基座模型中？
Mint Recursive在尝试的就是 让企业建立起自己的评测体系、奖励机制、训练数据，把后训练做成一个持续迭代的闭环 ：模型在服务用户后积累下真实任务场景数据，每次交互的轨迹，无论成功还是失败，都会被完整记录下来。
这其中，失败的轨迹相当有价值，哪里做错了、为什么错、应该怎么改，平台在找到问题和解决方法后，这些判断和轨迹会直接变成新的训练数据；用新数据重新训练完上线后，又会产生新的反馈，新的反馈又变成下一轮训练的输入，如此循环往复。
平台中的Env Hub（环境）环节容易被忽略，但它尤其关键。英伟达的一篇Agentic RL技术博客中提到，做Agent强化学习需要环境来定义数据集、验证器和状态。环境不只是模型的训练场，也是评测场，评测、合成数据、强化学习，都可以在一套环境中完成。
尽管Mint Recursive中的Recursive（递归）还处于初级形态——人依然在递归的回路中，离模型全自动自己训练还比较遥远，但模型迭代方向已经很明确了。对客户而言，更为重要的不是模型本身，而是企业手里的一线业务现场与独一无二的真实业务数据。

items.title: Steal My Food Itinerary: A Long Weekend in Upstate New York
items.summary: I love New York City in the summer, especially this past one, but I grew up in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains. I’m in my late 20s, I rock climb, and I live
items.text:
I love New York City in the summer, especially this past one, but I grew up in the shadow of the Rocky Mountains. I’m in my late 20s, I rock climb, and I live in Brooklyn, so of course I have an upstate New York itinerary for you. My partner’s mom’s partner (yes) has a cabin in Accord, New York, that we’ve been lucky to house sit, and I’ve fully fallen in love with the Catskills. Over the past few months, I’ve been so grateful to escape for a few long weekends among the trees and the birds and the slightly cooler weather of the Hudson Valley.

When I tell people in the city about my trips upstate, they’re often surprised to hear me gush about the restaurants. And while I think you could make all your meals (the bounty at the farm stands and markets make cooking very dreamy up there) and still have a great time, I can also strongly make the case for a dining-focused trip. Here’s where to go.

Day 1: Friday

If you’re heading up from the city, there are a few transit options (a bus from Port Authority to New Paltz or Kingston, the Metro North to Poughkeepsie, Amtrak to Hudson), but you’ll want a car to get around once you’re in the Catskills. I journey upstate via a car, which we pick up in New Jersey; that means that I get to grab Corner Slice’s massive, pillowy garlic knots as a pre-trip snack. If you find yourself in the area, I recommend you do the same.

Lunch

Stop at Storm King Art Center to take in the outdoor sculptures or catch a concert (I saw Dev Hynes’ ensemble there this summer and it was one of the most beautiful shows I’ve ever been to). I know museum restaurants are better than ever these days, but readers of this newsletter would probably appreciate that you can bring your own food and picnic, so I say pack a lunch. Anything goes; I’ve seen Panda Express from the nearest rest stop in those fields.

Dinner

Drive a little farther north and you’ll hit New Paltz, your first introduction to the charms of Upstate. Grab dinner at Shorties, a self-described “bar for the whole family” that lives up to the premise with DJs every night and pinball. A kimchi-topped hot dog is my move, but yours could be green pozole stew, togarashi-rubbed wings, or prosciutto- and pepperoncini-topped nachos. For those who are driving, a bonus at this spot is that the N/A drinks are good, with fun ingredients like salted guava juice. If you’re staying for longer than a night or two and planning to cook, stop by the fishmonger Gadaleto’s for all your seafood needs, while you’re in New Paltz. And if you’re planning to climb, you can rent pads from Rock & Snow.

Drinks

I stay in the Accord area, where lodging ranges wildly, from cabin Airbnbs to a souped-up retro motel to the luxury hotel Inness. The latter has a lovely (but pricey) restaurant for a group. Take in the same vibe (and view of the sunset) right outside the restaurant from the outdoor bar, where you can sit on Adirondack chairs around the fire and pretend you’re one of the celebrity guests. For a night-in alternative, grab a bottle of natural wine at Bluebird Wine Shop, which is next to the cutest grocery store, Accord Market — I like to stop in and pick up pie or ice cream for at-home (in-cabin?) dessert and drinks.

Day 2: Saturday

Lunch

In the morning, grab a coffee and pastry from Black Dot Cafe on your way to a hike at Minnewaska State Park, which has many trail options of varying lengths and levels of difficulty. Alternatively, if you’re a climber, go to the Mohonk Preserve. Both are beautiful, and — crucially for our purposes here — close to a really great German restaurant for lunch. The Mountain Brauhaus is a scene. I’ve never seen the family-owned German restaurant not packed with people, and as soon as you’re inside, you’ll see why. The portions are massive; the dirndl-clad servers are charming and personable; slices of pumpernickel come with most dishes, and I’ve witnessed people try and then subsequently order a loaf to take home — it’s that good. Recount your jaunt in nature over a wienerschnitzel, some spaetzle, a wheat beer with a slice of lemon, and excellent people watching.

A Snack and an Activity

Skate off the schnitzel at Skate Time, a retro roller rink run by the people behind Bjorn Qorn. You’re here to skate, yes, but also to have some pierogies from Helena’s Pierogis (the pierogi shop’s brick-and-mortar location in Kerhonkson is cash-only, so it’s a bonus to me, a serial non-cash-haver, that you can enjoy them here under the glow of popcorn-funded lights).

Dinner

Westwind Orchard is a staple for me. I was one of those people who didn’t really understand the hype of a good summer tomato until I had a life-changing panzanella here a few years ago. The ambiance here is the main attraction — parents let their children run free in the fields, there’s sometimes salsa dancing and live music, you’re surrounded by apple trees. Still, the food is better than it needs to be and so what you want when you’re on a trip where nature is the focus: fresh, seasonal, and simple. Get the aforementioned panzanella and don’t decide between pizza or pasta; get both. I like the pappardelle and the seasonal pizza is reliably excellent (right now, it’s summer squash and blossoms). Westwind is a cidery, but if you’re like me and not the biggest cider fan, rest assured that there are also classic cocktails highlighting New York ingredients, like a Negroni Sbagliato with cider as the bubbly topper.

Day 3: Sunday

Breakfast

Head north to Kingston. Have a cortado and a frittata from Village Coffee and Goods, then make your way around the town, which is one of my favorites in the area and a shopping destination for antiques, records, vintage clothing, and books.

Lunch

Rosie General is my favorite all-day cafe. I always get a mortadella sandwich or a chile-crisp-topped egg toast here. Recently, I surveyed the room and realized it seemed like every sandwich had its own dedicated kind of bread (some on English muffins, some on ciabatta, some on baguettes) made in-house; I really admire that level of commitment to detail. I generally prefer an edible souvenir to a trinket, and the shoppy shop-esque pantry of homemade mustards, pickles, infused oils and vinegars is a great place to pick one up.

Afternoon Pit Stops

Many NYC people travel upstate just to go to Stissing House; us included. On the way, we discovered Zabriskie’s Waterfall near the Bard College campus. It’s a swimming hole, but the vibe is more lean against a rock and read. When happy hour comes around, check out C. Cassis. You might associate cassis with old-timey France, but C. Cassis is doing it differently. Here, the blackcurrant liqueur isn’t sticky sweet, and you can enjoy it in fun applications like a piña colada, while learning more about the ingredient from friendly bartenders.

Dinner

Waiting for your table at Stissing House is actually part of the fun, because if you come sans reservation, you’re offered a seat and a drink in a living room-like space with candles and serve-yourself peanuts. I happily sipped a martini there, humming music from The Testament of Ann Lee (it’s very that vibe, honestly), awaiting a dinner of ham and pickles, fish pie, and steak. Skip dessert here (it’s fine, but I have a better plan). Back in the Accord area, hit Cherries Roadside; it’s classic Americana in a way that I have to say speaks to me. There is ice cream, sundaes, and milkshakes, but I always go with vanilla soft-serve — enjoy while marveling at the fact that you didn’t have to wait in one of the absurdly long froyo lines back in the city.

Honorable Mentions (and Where I Want to Hit Next Time

Harana Market makes some of my favorite Filipino food in the United States; they no longer have a dining room, but watch for pop-ups or takeaway opportunities (or if you have a big enough group, get catering!). Eng’s Chinese in Kingston is a slice of local history; I’ve so far only gotten (great) takeout, but I want to check out its dining room next. I recently had a head cheese sandwich from Cafe Mutton, in Hudson, that rocked my world. And if you are wine-inclined, Kingston Wine Co. sells some of the coolest bottles in the state, and Mirador, also in Kingston, is a great spot for sherry and pintxos. I’m also dying to check out the Oaxacan food scene in Poughkeepsie.

There are too many places to fit in one weekend, so I made you a list of more favorites in the Eater app. Follow me for more of my curated picks from the Northeast. (Subscribe to our travel newsletter, too!)

items.text:
美联储与特朗普之间的较量，正在进入最直接的对峙阶段。


美联储三年来首次加息，将联邦基金利率上调25个基点至3.75%至4%区间。特朗普随即公开要求将利率压至1%甚至更低，并指控美联储"出于政治目的"与他作对。美联储主席沃什在新闻发布会上明确回应：通胀已连续逾五年超出目标，此次加息决定符合美联储双重使命，且为委员会一致通过。


这场对峙的实质，是一个基本面尚属强健的经济体，与一届在财政、关税和地缘政策上持续冒进的政府之间的结构性张力。美联储选择坚守，而特朗普的1%利率主张，在当前宏观环境下既无依据，也难以落地。

三年来首次加息，沃什以"通胀超标"为由

美联储于上周宣布加息25个基点，这是三年来的首次上调。沃什在随后的新闻发布会上给出了两个核心论据：其一，通胀已连续超过五年运行在目标上方，价格稳定是当前政策的优先侧重；其二，美国经济目前呈现强化态势，在此背景下适度移除宽松立场具有必要性。


这一决定不仅是政策方向的转变，也是对市场信号的直接回应。9月17日，10年期通胀保值债券（TIPS）收益率约为2.6%，传统10年期国债收益率约为4.9%，由此隐含的通胀补偿约为2.3%。从历史维度看，名义收益率和实际收益率均大致回归至2007年至2009年金融危机前水平，结合近期经济表现，当前收益率水平处于合理区间。


更值得关注的是，沃什拒绝在任何层面——无论是政策立场还是修辞措辞——对特朗普的大幅降息诉求给予支持或背书。加息决定最终为委员会全票通过，展现出机构内部的高度统一。

特朗普的1%主张：逻辑站不住脚

特朗普在社交媒体上表示，美国是"世界上信用最好的国家"，利率"应当为1%甚至更低"，并指责美联储加息纯属"针对特朗普的政治行为"。他还透露，曾告知沃什"不如跟着委员会投票，因为结果不会有什么不同"。


然而，短期政策利率的决定逻辑与一国信用评级并无直接关联。短端利率由通货膨胀与失业率等宏观变量驱动，而非国家信用等级。长端名义利率则由实际利率、预期通胀及各类风险溢价共同决定。在当前通胀仍高于目标、财政赤字居高不下的背景下，将政策利率压至1%意味着实际利率约为负2%，这一水平极可能引发债权人的抗议乃至借贷罢工。


此外，"美国是世界最佳信用"这一表述本身也值得审视。"credit"一词源自拉丁语"credere"，意为"相信"。美国拥有全球最大且最具活力的经济体，但其政府的可信度正因特朗普政府持续突破规则的财政与关税政策而承压。分析人士指出，鉴于巨额财政赤字、对外部融资的高度依赖，以及债券持有结构从长期持有者向对冲基金转移的趋势，融资危机并非不可想象。

通胀长期超标与政策乘数：多重压力叠加

从更宏观的视角审视，自2021年以来，无论是整体通胀还是核心通胀指标，均持续运行于目标上方。与此同时，人工智能投资浪潮带来的需求扩张、特朗普政府的宽松财政立场、加征关税的供给侧冲击，以及对伊战争引发的能量价格冲击，多重因素叠加，使得通胀自然回落的前景更加不确定，压力方向反而指向上行。


在此背景下，部分观察人士对沃什的货币政策框架提出了实质性质疑。知名经济学家Claudia Sahm在其Substack专栏中提出几个关键问题：货币政策究竟通过何种机制促进增长？偏紧的货币政策若非通过压制经济活动，还有哪些路径可以压低通胀？沃什对"中性利率"是否有清晰的判断？若无，又如何评估当前政策的宽松程度？这些问题悬而未决，是外界观察沃什联储的重要观测维度。


不过，沃什对经济可预测性持审慎态度，这在一定程度上也与批评者的部分关切形成了方法论层面的分歧，而非全然背离。

央行独立性测压：最终考验尚未到来

当前这场对峙，折射出的是一个更深层的结构性命题：一个基本面尚属稳健的经济体，如何应对一届在财政和政策上持续越界的政府。美联储的职责在于不受政治压力干扰，维护通胀目标的可信度；而特朗普政府的施压，正在将这一职责置于公开检验之下。


沃什目前的立场是维持常规货币政策框架，不对政治压力让步。一致通过的加息决定，在机构信号层面具有重要意义。但正如分析人士所指出的，这场博弈的真正考验或许尚未到来——在财政压力与通胀压力双双走高的情景下，美联储能否持续坚守，将是决定这场较量最终走向的核心变量。

items.title: The 12 Essential Kitchen Tools for Beginners, According to Cooking Instructors

items.text:
Every time I see a meat tenderizer, I think of my mother. Specifically of the way in which she, as someone wary of emotional vulnerability yet full of affection (classic Boomer combo), decided to make Austrian pork schnitzel her love language — and the meat tenderizer her translator. In hindsight, that steel hammer was one of the best, most essential cooking tools in our home; it was also a beginner-friendly tool for me, a Montessori kid used to playing with saws at recess and expressing my feelings via dried bean art.

That tenderizer has become a staple of my kitchen ecosystem today. But one person’s tenderizer is another’s hand-me-down whisk, Japanese chef’s knife, or grill press. So what do other people consider their ride-or-die cooking tools? What are the baseline peelers, knives, and spatulas that are in constant rotation, the tools that make you feel like a culinary John Wick? I decided to ask not just chefs, but chefs with culinary school teaching experience (aka endless patience and a knowledge of novice-level skillsets) about what they consider to be the best beginner cooking tools.

In addition to a few of my own cooking essentials, I picked the brains of four teachers with experience in a variety of programs, from Hot Bread Kitchen — a New York City nonprofit that helps immigrants break into the food industry — to the legendary Institute of Culinary Education, all in the hopes of answering the inherently relative question of what constitutes an essential cooking tool for beginners.

Whether or not your new kitchen workhorse is destined to become an heirloom, some dos and don’ts for your search…

Do: Look for tools that don’t just do one thing.

Do: Read product reviews.

Don’t: Spend more than you need to on, say, a pair of tongs. And if you’re lucky enough to have a grandpa with a sick filet knife, maybe ask him about it.

First, grab a meat tenderizer.


Kitexpert Meat Tenderizer

Where to Buy:

$14.99 $11.98 at Amazon


Now, let’s talk essentials.

The best beginner cooking tools, according to Hot Bread Kitchen culinary teachers

Hot Bread Kitchen is a NYC-based culinary institute whose goal is to “uplift women, gender-expansive people, immigrants, and people of color” by helping them launch their careers in the food industry through intensive culinary training. Culinary instructors Kandy Williams and Charlene Johnson are two of the organization’s many acclaimed teachers, and they had some choice advice on the best beginner cooking tools.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Hot Bread Kitchen (@hotbreadkitchen)


A great spatula

“Spatulas are often one of the first tools that I introduce to my kids to learn to use when cooking because they’re safe and easy to handle,” says Williams. “It’s your all-in-one tool — perfect for flipping, stirring, and scraping every bit of batter from a bowl.”

“I love to use a silicone spatula to gently fold ingredients like egg whites into batter,” Williams goes on. “As a baker, this is one of my favorite tools in the kitchen. I use it all the time when I prepare my buttercreams, cakes, and alfajores (Peruvian macarons). This keeps the mixture light and fluffy.”

Johnson seconds the tool’s utility for not only whipping up meals, but also allowing you to store your leftovers and ingredients. “It will allow you to get every bit of your food from containers,” she says, “to where they need to be — in your belly!”

Reach for a BPA-free silicone spatula such as this high-rated option that costs less than an order of avocado toast. It’s heat-resistant up to 600 degrees Fahrenheit, has a stainless steel internal frame — just like RoboCop — and a slightly curved blade for scraping and folding with precision.


DI ORO Silicone Spatula

Where to Buy:

$13.97 at Amazon


A workhouse vegetable peeler

At home, Williams relies on a high-quality peeler to prep everything from mashed potatoes to causa peruana with her kids; it makes prep work much faster for her students and more efficient for her as a culinary instructor. “I always show how to use a peeler safely by peeling away from the body and using short, controlled strokes. They use it to peel potatoes, carrots, butternut squash, and more vegetables. It’s also a great tool to introduce them to different textures.”

Johnson also swears by the power of the classic Swiss peeler, specifically — and not just for veggies. “It’s efficient and precise,” she says. “Use it on chocolate, cheese, or citrus. Get creative. FYI, the purpose of the protruding circle to the side of the peeler is to remove potato eyes.”

Williams Sonoma’s straight swivel-action, steel blade peeler contours to the shape of whatever potato, pear, or state fair butter sculpture you’re peeling:


Williams Sonoma Prep Tools Straight Swivel Peeler

Where to Buy:

$22.95 at Williams Sonoma


For a classic Swiss peeler, you can’t go wrong with a Victorinox straight blade, which has been GOATed by many. It’s peeler is lightweight, is made with a nonslip textured handle, and is under $10 on Amazon.


Victorinox straight-blade peeler

Where to Buy:

$9 at Amazon


A solid paring knife

As Williams says, a paring knife is “small and versatile, perfect for tasks that require precision, like peeling, trimming, or slicing small fruits and veggies.” She introduces the tool to beginner students to use for more delicate tasks — such as cutting strawberries, scoring tomatoes, or trimming herbs — in order to build their knife skills safely. “In classes my students use a paring knife to practice the concasse technique,” she says, “They love to prepare ratatouille. The paring knife is often called the ‘extension of the hand’ because it’s so maneuverable.”

Quality knives can be a costly investment, but beginners will appreciate the affordable paring knife from Quince. Its 3.5-inch paring knife is made out of 33 layers of Japanese Damascus stainless steel — which helps it achieve excellent blade balance — and it features a naturally water-resistant Pakkawood handle.


Quince Essential Japanese Damascus steel 3.5” paring knife

Where to Buy:

$39.9 at Quince


An offset serrated knife

Johnson says her serrated knife is key for cutting bread, slicing tomatoes, and more. “It’s great for anything that has a tough exterior and soft interior,” she explains. “The offset handle provides space so that the blade hits the cutting board before my hand. Efficient and delivers stellar results. 10 out of 10.”

This 9-inch offset blade sports an ergonomic handle and a serrated blade that does the job of the fancier versions at an entry-level price.


Mercer Culinary Offset Bread Knife

Where to Buy:

$27.99 at Amazon


The best beginner cooking tools, according to Celine Beitchman of the Institute of Culinary Education

The Institute of Culinary Education (ICE) was founded in 1975, and is ranked as the number-one culinary school in the United States, with locations in New York City and Los Angeles. Celine Beitchman, director of nutrition, tells me that she has been “teaching health-promoting culinary arts for about a decade,” and “became a chef over a 20-year period working in prep kitchens, restaurants, catering, and as a private chef,” first at the Natural Gourmet Institute and now within ICE’s Plant-Based Culinary Arts program.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Institute of Culinary Education (@iceculinary)


A big, sharp chef’s knife

If you don’t know where to begin with your own knife drawer, Beitchman recommends starting with an 8- to 10-inch chef’s knife. As she says, “It’s vital to handle most of the essential vegetable cuts, and for slicing everything from cheese to cake. A good knife will last, and it’s worth investing in one that you are comfortable using — one that’s not too long or heavy for you.” Check out our full guide to the best chef’s knives here, for every budget and purpose.

One of my first kitchen knives was a Made In blade, and I remember thinking, Wow, so this is what it feels like to hold a knife with its own backbone. Or, maybe what I was feeling was the single rod of stainless steel that extends from tip to handle, which is what the brand claims sets it apart. Years later, my 8-inch Made In chef’s knife still chops everything from crunchy cabbage to a tarte tatin with ease, despite my less-than-perfect knife skills.


Made In 8-inch chef’s knife

Where to Buy:

$129 $99.99 at Made In


If you’re shopping on more of a budget, I also can’t recommend Imarku’s chef’s knife enough. This 8-inch stainless steel blade cuts with as much precision as some of my friends’ fancy Wüsthof knives, but it costs under $50. I do need to sharpen it more frequently than some pricier knives (I find that the sweet spot is around every two months), but you really can’t beat the bang for your buck on this sucker. Plus, it ships in a secure, velvet-esque-lined box that makes for a thoughtful (last-minute) housewarming gift.


Imarku Japanese Chef’s Knife (8-Inch)

Where to Buy:

$39.99 at Amazon


Spring-loaded tongs

“Spring-loaded tongs with metal or rubber-coated tips can be used to toss salads in dressings or vegetables in seasonings before they hit the oven,” says Beitchman. “When I started cooking, tongs were almost an extension of my own hand and they let me reach further down the stove or up to the salamander.”

These stainless 12-inch long steel tongs come from one of my favorite affordable cookware brands, OXO. Scalloped edges are a big plus for me when it comes to tongs, because they allow for better precision and grip when I’m flipping whole padrón peppers on the grill or prodding my veggies around in a skillet. Plus, the slight concave of the tongs make it easy to ladle excess oils or sauce from a pan, (which I love to do when I’m frying eggs in chile crisp).


Oxo stainless steel tongs

Where to Buy:

$14.99 at Wayfair


Bench scraper

Finally, Beitchman stands by the power of the bench scraper. “[Bench scrapers] are amazingly versatile,” she says, “and can be used to move and lift food off of cutting boards and trays, to scrape flours and shape loaves before baking,” and more.

Crate & Barrel has gone the extra mile with this stainless steel bench scraper, which includes not only a soft-touch plastic handle that won’t slip from your grip, but a sweet little built-in ruler. It’s always a plus when a kitchen staple can combine more than one tool or function, and being able to measure out and chop your dough with one hand is a clutch time saver.


Crate & Barrel bench scraper

Where to Buy:

$19.95 at Crate & Barrel


The best beginner cooking tools, according to chef Vanessa Seder

Vanessa Seder has worked as a chef, food stylist, cookbook author, and associate food editor at Ladies’ Home Journal — to name just a handful of her culinary accomplishments — in addition to teaching for many years at the storied Stonewall Kitchen Headquarters in York, Maine. She, too, sang the praises of sharp chef’s knives and different-sized spatulas, but she also recommended a few more less-obvious tools.


View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Vanessa Seder (@vanessa_seder_eats)


A high-quality wood cutting board

It seems easy enough to remember, but a quality cutting board can sometimes go overlooked when you’re outfitting your kitchen with beginner cooking tools and equipment. Seder recommends John Boos & Co., one of the oldest manufacturers of butcher blocks in the country. She says that she loves the sturdy feel of her Boos board, which is 1.5 inches thick and perfect for rolling out dough while baking or making pasta, and also gives the board a bit of a height boost — a plus that she appreciates, she says, given that she’s on the taller side and doesn’t want to slouch while chopping or rolling herbs. It’s also quite a looker in terms of items that can take up precious real estate on your kitchen counters. As Seder says, “I use it sometimes as a cheese platter when we have guests over.”


John Boos Cutting Board (20” x 15”, Cherry Wood)

Where to Buy:

$158.95 at Amazon


A whetstone for sharpening knives

Those paring and chef’s knives aren’t going to sharpen themselves. As Seder says, “Learning how to sharpen your knives will save you money and time in the long run. A sharp knife is safer to use in that it prevents slippage, which can result in injury.” But getting your knives sharpened professionally can really add up in cost, she adds, so throwing down for a whetstone can be a great long-term investment. Consider this Japanese-made ceramic whetstone by King, which only costs about $50. There’s a dedicated Eater guide to sharpening your knives like a pro, but suffice to say this kit comes with everything you need: a 1000/6000 grit combination whetstone (with the former for main sharpening and the latter for finish sharpening), an angle holder for blade-sharpening accuracy, and a quick-drying cloth.


King whetstone

Where to Buy:

$52.99 at Amazon


A fish spatula

Seder says that she still has her fish spatula from culinary school, a trusty Wüsthof that continues to go the distance. This 6.5-inch slotted fish spatula from the German brand is about more than just fish, and acts as a flexible tool for cooking not only fish, but anything delicate. The Wüsthof version has earned heaps of praise for its being lightweight, angled, and slotted, which allows excess oils to drain through when you’re moving things around. Or as one reviewer writes, “Sometimes it is the small things in life that give you the motivation to be a better cook.” Our thoughts exactly.

Look in any commercial kitchen, and you’ll see stainless steel, stainless steel, stainless steel. Why? Because stainless steel cookware is durable, versatile, and has great heat conductivity and retention.

That’s why we took our collaboration with Heritage Steel seriously; our high-quality, 5-ply stainless steel pans are ready to take on any and all cooking projects, from perfect pancakes to sunny-side-up eggs to seared salmon (in which case the spatula above will come in handy). The 12-inch pan is the perfect do-everything size, while the 3-quart saucier (which also comes with a lid) can cook pasta, poach eggs, and so much more.

blocks.x: Every time I see a meat tenderizer, I think of my mother. Specifically of the way in which she, as someone wary of emotional vulnerability yet full of affection (classic Boomer combo), decided to make Austrian pork schnitzel her love language — and the meat tenderizer her translator. In hindsight, that steel hammer was one of the best, most essential cooking tools in our home; it was also a beginner-friendly tool for me, a Montessori kid used to playing with saws at recess and expressing my feelings via dried bean art.

That tenderizer has become a staple of my kitchen ecosystem today. But one person’s tenderizer is another’s hand-me-down whisk, Japanese chef’s knife, or grill press. So what do other people consider their ride-or-die cooking tools? What are the baseline peelers, knives, and spatulas that are in constant rotation, the tools that make you feel like a culinary John Wick? I decided to ask not just chefs, but chefs with culinary school teaching experience (aka endless patience and a knowledge of novice-level skillsets) about what they consider to be the best beginner cooking tools.

In addition to a few of my own cooking essentials, I picked the brains of four teachers with experience in a variety of programs, from Hot Bread Kitchen — a New York City nonprofit that helps immigrants break into the food industry — to the legendary Institute of Culinary Education, all in the hopes of answering the inherently relative question of what constitutes an essential cooking tool for beginners.
Whether or not your new kitchen workhorse is destined to become an heirloom, some dos and don’ts for your search…
Do: Look for tools that don’t just do one thing.
Do: Read product reviews.
Don’t: Spend more than you need to on, say, a pair of tongs. And if you’re lucky enough to have a grandpa with a sick filet knife, maybe ask him about it.
First, grab a meat tenderizer.
Kitexpert Meat Tenderizer
Where to Buy:
$14.99 $11.98 at Amazon
Now, let’s talk essentials.
The best beginner cooking tools, according to Hot Bread Kitchen culinary teachers

Hot Bread Kitchen is a NYC-based culinary institute whose goal is to “uplift women, gender-expansive people, immigrants, and people of color” by helping them launch their careers in the food industry through intensive culinary training. Culinary instructors Kandy Williams and Charlene Johnson are two of the organization’s many acclaimed teachers, and they had some choice advice on the best beginner cooking tools.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by Hot Bread Kitchen (@hotbreadkitchen)
A great spatula

“Spatulas are often one of the first tools that I introduce to my kids to learn to use when cooking because they’re safe and easy to handle,” says Williams. “It’s your all-in-one tool — perfect for flipping, stirring, and scraping every bit of batter from a bowl.”

“I love to use a silicone spatula to gently fold ingredients like egg whites into batter,” Williams goes on. “As a baker, this is one of my favorite tools in the kitchen. I use it all the time when I prepare my buttercreams, cakes, and alfajores (Peruvian macarons). This keeps the mixture light and fluffy.”

Johnson seconds the tool’s utility for not only whipping up meals, but also allowing you to store your leftovers and ingredients. “It will allow you to get every bit of your food from containers,” she says, “to where they need to be — in your belly!”

Reach for a BPA-free silicone spatula such as this high-rated option that costs less than an order of avocado toast. It’s heat-resistant up to 600 degrees Fahrenheit, has a stainless steel internal frame — just like RoboCop — and a slightly curved blade for scraping and folding with precision.
DI ORO Silicone Spatula
Where to Buy:
$13.97 at Amazon
A workhouse vegetable peeler

At home, Williams relies on a high-quality peeler to prep everything from mashed potatoes to causa peruana with her kids; it makes prep work much faster for her students and more efficient for her as a culinary instructor. “I always show how to use a peeler safely by peeling away from the body and using short, controlled strokes. They use it to peel potatoes, carrots, butternut squash, and more vegetables. It’s also a great tool to introduce them to different textures.”

Johnson also swears by the power of the classic Swiss peeler, specifically — and not just for veggies. “It’s efficient and precise,” she says. “Use it on chocolate, cheese, or citrus. Get creative. FYI, the purpose of the protruding circle to the side of the peeler is to remove potato eyes.”
Williams Sonoma’s straight swivel-action, steel blade peeler contours to the shape of whatever potato, pear, or state fair butter sculpture you’re peeling:
Williams Sonoma Prep Tools Straight Swivel Peeler
Where to Buy:
$22.95 at Williams Sonoma

For a classic Swiss peeler, you can’t go wrong with a Victorinox straight blade, which has been GOATed by many. It’s peeler is lightweight, is made with a nonslip textured handle, and is under $10 on Amazon.
Victorinox straight-blade peeler
Where to Buy:
$9 at Amazon
A solid paring knife

As Williams says, a paring knife is “small and versatile, perfect for tasks that require precision, like peeling, trimming, or slicing small fruits and veggies.” She introduces the tool to beginner students to use for more delicate tasks — such as cutting strawberries, scoring tomatoes, or trimming herbs — in order to build their knife skills safely. “In classes my students use a paring knife to practice the concasse technique,” she says, “They love to prepare ratatouille. The paring knife is often called the ‘extension of the hand’ because it’s so maneuverable.”

Quality knives can be a costly investment, but beginners will appreciate the affordable paring knife from Quince. Its 3.5-inch paring knife is made out of 33 layers of Japanese Damascus stainless steel — which helps it achieve excellent blade balance — and it features a naturally water-resistant Pakkawood handle.
Quince Essential Japanese Damascus steel 3.5” paring knife
Where to Buy:
$39.9 at Quince
An offset serrated knife

Johnson says her serrated knife is key for cutting bread, slicing tomatoes, and more. “It’s great for anything that has a tough exterior and soft interior,” she explains. “The offset handle provides space so that the blade hits the cutting board before my hand. Efficient and delivers stellar results. 10 out of 10.”
This 9-inch offset blade sports an ergonomic handle and a serrated blade that does the job of the fancier versions at an entry-level price.
Mercer Culinary Offset Bread Knife
Where to Buy:
$27.99 at Amazon
The best beginner cooking tools, according to Celine Beitchman of the Institute of Culinary Education

The Institute of Culinary Education (ICE) was founded in 1975, and is ranked as the number-one culinary school in the United States, with locations in New York City and Los Angeles. Celine Beitchman, director of nutrition, tells me that she has been “teaching health-promoting culinary arts for about a decade,” and “became a chef over a 20-year period working in prep kitchens, restaurants, catering, and as a private chef,” first at the Natural Gourmet Institute and now within ICE’s Plant-Based Culinary Arts program.
View this post on Instagram
A post shared by Institute of Culinary Education (@iceculinary)
A big, sharp chef’s knife

If you don’t know where to begin with your own knife drawer, Beitchman recommends starting with an 8- to 10-inch chef’s knife. As she says, “It’s vital to handle most of the essential vegetable cuts, and for slicing everything from cheese to cake. One of my first kitchen knives was a Made In blade, and I remember thinking, Wow, so this is what it feels like to hold a knife with its own backbone. Or, maybe what I was feeling was the single rod of stainless steel that extends from tip to handle, which is what the brand claims sets it apart. Years later, my 8-inch Made In chef’s knife still chops everything from crunchy cabbage to a tarte tatin with ease, despite my less-than-perfect knife skills.
Made In 8-inch chef’s knife
Where to Buy:
$129 $99.99 at Made In

If you’re shopping on more of a budget, I also can’t recommend Imarku’s chef’s knife enough. This 8-inch stainless steel blade cuts with as much precision as some of my friends’ fancy Wüsthof knives, but it costs under $50. I do need to sharpen it more frequently than some pricier knives (I find that the sweet spot is around every two months), but you really can’t beat the bang for your buck on this sucker. Plus, it ships in a secure, velvet-esque-lined box that makes for a thoughtful (last-minute) housewarming gift.
Imarku Japanese Chef’s Knife (8-Inch)
Where to Buy:
$39.99 at Amazon
Spring-loaded tongs

“Spring-loaded tongs with metal or rubber-coated tips can be used to toss salads in dressings or vegetables in seasonings before they hit the oven,” says Beitchman. “When I started cooking, tongs were almost an extension of my own hand and they let me reach further down the stove or up to the salamander.”

Oxo stainless steel tongs

$14.99 at Wayfair

It’s always a plus when a kitchen staple can combine more than one tool or function, and being able to measure out and chop your dough with one hand is a clutch time saver.
Crate & Barrel bench scraper

$19.95 at Crate & Barrel

items.title: Unusual Picnic Places Around the World
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: There’s nothing quite like a picnic surrounded by friends and family, soaking in the sun, sharing snacks, and enjoying the sounds of nature. Whether you prefer
items.text:
There’s nothing quite like a picnic surrounded by friends and family, soaking in the sun, sharing snacks, and enjoying the sounds of nature. Whether you prefer to use one big blanket, sit at a table with benches, or plop right onto the grass, it’s the perfect good-weather get together (and a great excuse to load up on delicious food).


With this guide, you’ll find a picnic spot that’s guaranteed to impress your guests and spark envy in your enemies. These aren’t your average grassy fields; they’re oases colored by folklore stories, whimsical art, monumental moments in history, and otherworldly formations. From an abandoned power plant in the mountains of Mexico to a gold-mine-turned-swimming-hole in southern Australia, these are the best places across the globe for an unforgettable outdoor meal.

1. Old Zoo Picnic Area 📍 Los Angeles, California


The first Los Angeles Zoo may have closed in the 1960s, but remnants still remain in Griffith Park, where they’re now outfitted with picnic tables and grills. Peek inside abandoned monkey cages and walk through the bear grotto in between bites, or wander a trail up from the caves for a view of what was once the lion dens.

2. Sports City 📍 Amman, Jordan


This crumbling sporting complex, once the training ground for elite athletes, now consists of drained swimming pools, empty gymnasiums, and overgrown tracks. However, that doesn’t mean it’s gone unused; in a city where public green space is a rarity, the complex has become a popular spot for picnics, hookah smoking, and simply sprawling in the shade.

3. Ras Angela 📍 Ras Angela, Tunisia


The rocky head of Ras Angela, or Cape Angela, juts out into the Mediterranean Sea, forming what is considered to the northernmost point of Africa. Marked with a Tunisian flag and a sculpture of the continent, it is a peaceful spot to enjoy a picnic and ocean views. You can also lay out your towel on the adjacent sandy beach and take a dip into the perfectly blue water.

4. Bomi Blue Lake 📍 Tubmanburg, Liberia


When the Liberia Mining Company abandoned its operations here in the late 1970s, it left behind a series of pit mines, which eventually filled with spring water to become a single beautiful lake. With clear, unpolluted waters, the lake is open for swimming, and the wooden pavilions around its perimeter are great for picnics.


5. Christy Buchanan’s SHE Garden & Gallery 📍 Winnsboro, South Carolina


This whimsical folk garden was created by artist and architect Christy Buchanan, who dreamed up a space that would reflect the nuanced beauty of everyday found objects. Visitors can have a picnic in the Love Shack, take pictures under the bicycle arch, or commune with ancestors in the Tiki hut. Buchanan also constantly adds to the site, so you’re sure to spy new works each time you visit. If her SUV (nicknamed Happy) is in the yard, Buchanan is home, but feel free to stop by even if she isn’t.


6. Old Wardour Castle 📍 Tisbury, England


After being decimated in a 1642 siege, this castle’s military career ended; however, it has found a second life as a tourist attraction. Fully restored and transformed with neat landscaping, the estate is now a favorite spot for picnics, weddings, and even film crews. Visitors to the castle can still climb the worn tower stairs for a sweeping view of the English countryside or lounge in the same sun-soaked courtyard that English barons once frequented.

7. Woolshed Falls 📍 Beechworth, Australia


Once the center of a massive, 19th-century mining enterprise, these falls have since been reclaimed by nature, with channels worn into the rock forming natural showers, baths and waterslides. There’s also a plunge pool at the end of the falls, unusually deep for its size thanks to the large amount of gold removed from the silty bottom.


Accessible by two different walking paths, the falls are a pleasant, family-friendly spot for picnics, swimming, and rock jumping (though children should be closely supervised).

8. Tuzluca Salt Mines 📍 Tuzluca, Turkey


The Tuz Mağarası, or Tuzluca Salt Caves, have supplied salt to this region since medieval times, though they only recently opened to the public. Now, anyone who’s not too claustrophobic can walk a boardwalk through the curving, cavernous interior. Warm lighting lends the dark space a cozy atmosphere, and picnic tables set around the chamber walls invite visitors to set up camp and stay a while.


9. Gravelly Point Park 📍 Arlington, Virginia


Most aircraft approaching Washington National Airport loop over this small Arlington park in their final descent, and locals gather for the spectacle of roaring engines, screeching wheels, and the unmistakable scent of burnt rubber on the runway. With plenty of wide open space for kids to run around and close-up views of the Potomac River, Gravelly Point is the perfect place to spend an afternoon munching on snacks and staring up at the clouds.


10. La Planta 📍 San Agustín Etla, Mexico


On the mountainside above San Agustín Etla, this former water-powered electric power plant is now a popular spot for hikers and picnickers to take in sweeping views of the city. A poem posted near the ruins reminds visitors of the importance of nature, proposing that the Earth’s resources are significantly more valuable than money: “Only after the last tree is cut ... only after the last river is poisoned ... only after the last fish is caught ... only then, you will understand ... that you cannot eat money.”

11. Al Wathba Fossil Dunes 📍 Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates


This area on the outskirts of Abu Dhabi was once covered by water. However, over time, as sediments settled at the bottom, the many mineral-heavy layers became compacted and cemented into stable structures. Since then, they’ve been further molded by winds and sediment into utterly unique shapes.


This seemingly-endless desert landscape is popular for early-morning picnics and also makes for a great camping spot. Just remember: The sand figures are incredibly fragile, so under no circumstances should you climb them.


12. Tiger Cave 📍 Mahabalipuram, India


Surrounded by swaying casuarina trees in the Bay of Bengal, Tiger Cave has long been a favored recreation spot among locals willing to make trek there from town. The site’s name comes from its crown of 11 tiger-esque heads carved around the entrance to its gaping maw. Archaeologists believe that the site likely once served as a portico from which rulers spoke or observed festivities.


The park’s grounds are maintained by the Archaeological Survey of India as a free, public space, and between its lush greenery and food and drink stands, it’s a pleasant spot for those seeking respite from Mahabalipuram’s busy streets.


13. Sa Stiddiosa 📍 Gadoni, Italy


A hike through the heart of Sardinia will lead you to this gentle waterfall, though its name actually translates from the Sardo dialect to “dripping” rather than “falling.” Local families descend into the valley to picnic, bathe in the Flumendosa River’s cool, shaded waters, and jump off the large boulder at the river’s center.


14. The Dick Lane Velodrome 📍 East Point, Georgia


Atlanta’s hub for all things cycling is a 1/5-mile track with 36-degree banked turns, which intrepid competitors race down at 40 miles an hour. Located in the city’s East Point neighborhood, the Velodrome has become a point of civic pride and local entertainment with its concession stand, public seating, picnic area, and plentiful green space. The East Point Velodrome Association runs activities on-site throughout the year, from bike safety clinics to a youth cycling league.

items.title: 12 Sculptures Made From Recycled Materials
items.author: Holyn Thigpen
items.summary: For time immemorial, human beings have generated trash ... lots and lots of trash. And from the aqueducts and municipal dumps of ancient times to the massive
items.text:
For time immemorial, human beings have generated trash ... lots and lots of trash. And from the aqueducts and municipal dumps of ancient times to the massive landfills of today, we’ve tried all kinds of ways to get rid of it. However, when trash makes its way into the right hands, it can be turned from mere waste into something imaginative and daring. Creative folks around the world have seen old materials as more than just their previous lives, looking instead to their futures.


These works show the truth of that age-old statement: “One man’s trash is another man’s treasure.” With materials ranging from old cars to scrap metal to glass bottles and discarded beach chairs, artists have gone above and beyond to reimagine how waste is thought about and used. 1. Tire Sculptures of Breighner’s Tire Center 📍 Littlestown, Pennsylvania


When Noah Russell, an employee at Breighner’s Tire Center, was challenged by his boss to build a tire float for a local parade, he created a massive lion that won first place. Riding this high, he entered the following year with an eight-foot-tall, fire-breathing dragon made out of coat hangers, turf tires, and a can of bucane.(Unsurprisingly, he won again.)


Russell followed these creations with an intricate headless horseman, a horned stag, and a reef with several aquatic animals. Along with the two prize-winning creatures, these spectacles now sit in front of Breighner’s storefront, where they’ve become a favorite landmark for people traveling along Hanover Pike.

2. Frontera Sculpture Oasis 📍 Luna County, New Mexico


This unique sculpture garden sits in the middle of the Chihuahuan desert, right on the U.S./Mexico border. Artist Taras Mychalewych created the work as a tribute to Mother Earth after his car blew up in the very same desert while he was on a cross-country drive.


The garden’s makeshift biosphere is formed out of scavenged and donated materials, from bricks to bottles, and was designed to mingle with the surrounding agave and cholla. One colorful display represents a regional mariachi band, welcoming people to the borderlands, while another portion feels directly inspired by Los Angeles’s Watts Towers. In its entirety, the isolated oasis acts as an ode to nature’s bounty but also a warning to those who have defiled it in the name of profit.

3. Rainbow Sea Container 📍 Fremantle, Australia


Situated between two bridges in a Perth suburb, this colorful sculpture pays homage to the area’s rich history as an industrial port. Locally nicknamed “The Containbow,” the nine sea containers are assembled into a striking, 29-foot-tall arch that can be spotted far and wide. Perth artist Marcus Cannin painted the containers all shades of the rainbow to recognize Fremont’s recently revitalized creative scene.

4. Badaren - Spår av Mänsklighet (The Swimmer - Traces of Man) 📍 Skanör med Falsterbo, Sweden


Nearly 200 discarded chairs and parasols, plus heaps of trash from nearby beaches, form this sculpture in a parking lot in southern Sweden. The installation serves as a reminder of the impact a single individual’s actions can have on the environment. Every single step of the lifecycle of the goods, from manufacturing to shipping and destruction, leaves an impact.

5. Volkswagen Spider Sculpture 📍 Palm Springs, California


This giant metal spider with a Volkswagen Beetle body stands outside Hole in the Wall, a former auto repair shop that’s now a hub of delightful desert eccentricity. The 28-foot-tall beast was built by Robert Miner, the shop’s longtime owner, who eventually moved onto the property and installed a treehouse/lookout tower (bedecked with spider/web motifs, naturally).

6. The Raven’s Nest 📍 Reykjavik, Iceland


On the outskirts of Iceland’s capital stand mammoth sculptures of discarded scrap metal, constantly evolving as new pieces are added. These are the work of Icelandic filmmaker Hrafn Gunnlaugsson, who bought the oceanside property in 1977 and immediately began transforming it into a surreal sculpture park.


“I was given the name Hrafn. That means raven, I think it goes with the name: Ravens like to collect things. Maybe I can blame the habit on my name,” Hafrn said of his unique hobby.


Gunnlaugsson’s home (itself a work of art) sits at the center of the site, looking out onto rusty Viking warriors, deities from around the world, totem poles formed from old ship parts, and a giant eyeball made out of a buoy.

7. Schaefer’s Auto Art 📍 Erie, Pennsylvania


For over 25 years, this roadside attraction has charmed visitors with its folksy sculptures, depicting everything from a bumblebee to an “automan” to a two-headed dinosaur. With these reimagined automobiles, Erie local Richard Schaefer has turned an otherwise quiet country road into a must-see attraction.

8. Blenko Man 📍 Weston, West Virginia


When the Museum of American Glass reopened in 2007 in a new location, this silica fellow became its mighty mascot. Rock Wilson, an avid collector of Blenko glass, commissioned renowned sculptor John Zidek to turn his collection into a tribute to West Virginia’s once-ubiquitous industry. Thus, Blenko Man was born.


As guardian and greeter for the museum, Blenko Man oversees a vast collection of practically every type of glass item imaginable, from a five-foot-tall stained glass dollhouse to a marble made in the first century AD. While he does, in fact, have two right feet (a manufacturing quirk in the original glassware used), this has just made him all the more iconic.

9. Ernesto Che Guevara Statue 📍 El Alto, Bolivia


In the very country where Che Guevara met his demise stands a 30-foot-tall statue of the dictator made out of engines, cogs, wheels, and other mechanical spare parts. Sculptor Felix Duran imbued the work with two unique features: First, Guevara is depicted stomping on a bald eagle (a clear allusion to his anti-American sentiments). Second, his face is distinctly indigenous. This latter choice has been interpreted in different ways; some view it as a cultural tribute, while others see it as the appropriation of local identity.

10. Árbol de la Sidra 📍 Gijón, Spain


Asturias, an autonomous community in northern Spain, is known for its traditional tart apple cider, served with great finesse at the region’s many sidrerías. In 2013, this artistic homage to the boozy beverage was unveiled in Gijón, where it is illuminated each night by a large lamp inside of it. According to a plaque near the sculpture, this unusual monument is a nod to the tree of life, as well as a visual representation of how natural resources can be preserved by reusing everyday objects.

11. Ethyl the Whale 📍 Santa Fe, New Mexico


At 82 feet long, this friendly whale holds the Guinness World Record for largest recycled plastic sculpture. Named for her polyethylene body, she was designed by two San Francisco artists, Yustina Salnikova and Joel Stockdill, to spread awareness of the negative impact plastics have on the environment.


Originally built for California’s Monterey Bay Aquarium, she was acquired by the New-Mexico-based art collective Meow Wolf in 2019 and transported to the middle of the desert, where she still receives many excited visitors.


12. Recycled Roadrunner Statue 📍 Las Cruces, New Mexico


At a scenic rest area, this massive roadrunner perches on a boulder, gazing over the city below. The sculpture is a whopping 20 feet tall and composed of old shoes, cell phones, bike parts, and other recycled materials. Designed by local artist Olin Calk in 1993, it first stood at the local landfill to draw attention to our poor consumption habits.

items.title: Beyond Colonial Williamsburg: 11 Events Worth Planning a Trip Around
items.author: Atlas Obscura

items.text:
The Historic Triangle is often associated with powdered wigs, Revolutionary War reenactments, and America’s founding story. But between Williamsburg, Yorktown, and Jamestown, the year is filled with celebrations that span far beyond the 18th century. You can spend a January weekend listening to world-class jazz, cheer a parade of illuminated boats, or deliciously discover why Williamsburg proudly calls itself the “Pancake Capital of the World.”


Whether you’re planning a weekend getaway or a longer stay, these annual events showcase the area’s contemporary culture alongside its historic roots.


1. The Great American Birthday Quilt Exhibition (All Year)

Most quilts tell the story of a family. Williamsburg’s newest quilt tells the story of a country.


Created to commemorate America’s 250th anniversary, the Great American Birthday Quilt is a 1,000-foot-long fabric artwork assembled from quilt squares contributed by people across the United States. Assisted by artist Steve Prince of the Muscarelle Museum of Art at William & Mary, the project invited individuals, families, students, veterans, and community groups to create pieces reflecting their own connections to the American story.


The result is a national patchwork of thousands of individual memories, symbols, and designs stitched into one enormous textile. Visitors can see rotating sections of the quilt throughout 2026 at the Colonial Williamsburg Regional Visitor Center, the Greater WIlliamsburg Sports and Events Center, and the Muscarelle Museum of Art.


2. Pancake Trail in the “Pancake Capital of the World”

While pancakes might feel like a modern dish, they’re also a piece of the past. In 2025, Frank Clark, master of historic foodways at Colonial Williamsburg, told Garden & Gun, “Pancakes were quite popular in the Colonial period because they were simply cake in a pan.”


Pancakes have come a long way since the 18th century, evolving from humble hoecakes to syrup-drenched gargantuan stacks of buttermilk and buckwheat that we eat for breakfast today. This is especially apparent in Williamsburg, a city so packed with pancake houses—from Capitol Pancake to Colonial Pancake House to Mama Steve’s—it’s dubbed itself the “Pancake Capital of the World.”


Every year, Williamsburg celebrates its plethora of pancakes with a festival filled with pancake breakfasts, eating competitions, and a “Pancake Trail” that leads visitors on a crawl across some of the city’s best flapjack-slinging spots.


3. Winter Blues Jazz Fest

Williamsburg may be best known for colonial history, but every Martin Luther King Jr. weekend the city turns its attention to a more modern art form: jazz. Since its founding in 2015, the Winter Blues Jazz Fest has welcomed artists ranging from the six-time Grammy-winning Blind Boys of Alabama and Chicago blues guitarist Wayne Baker Brooks to vocalist Tahira Clayton, jazz drummer Jae Sinnett, and hometown swing favorites Good Shot Judy.


The festival reflects the musical traditions of Virginia’s Tidewater region, where jazz, blues, gospel, and church music have long overlapped. Concerts unfold in venues ranging from the William & Mary Alumni House to the Historic First Baptist Church, alongside workshops, brunch concerts, and evening jam sessions. The result feels less like a conventional music festival and more like a citywide celebration of blues and jazz.


4. Last Word Comedy Festival

Williamsburg may be best known for faithfully recreating the 18th century, but each January it celebrates an art form built entirely on the unexpected. The Last Word Comedy Festival brings together improvisers, sketch performers, stand-up comics, and musical comedians from across North America for four days of performances that prove spontaneity can be just as captivating as historical reenactment.


The lineup has featured comedy heavyweights, including “Whose Live Anyway?” (starring Ryan Stiles, Greg Proops, Jeff B. Davis, Joel Murray, and Laura Hall) as well as Bluebird Improv, whose performers include “Saturday Night Live” alumnus Tim Meadows and “Veep” star Matt Walsh. Alongside these nationally known acts, audiences can discover experimental improv troupes, fully improvised musicals, and collegiate ensembles from William & Mary and universities across the region.


The festival’s intimate scale is part of its charm. Rather than anchoring itself in a single convention center, performances unfold across theaters, breweries, and performance spaces in downtown Williamsburg, allowing visitors to hop from one show to the next over the course of an evening.


5. Virginia Black Film Festival

Every February, the Virginia Black Film Festival brings independent filmmakers, actors, and audiences together for screenings, conversations, and workshops celebrating Black cinema. Founded by filmmaker Bryan G. Thompson, the festival was created to give Black storytellers a larger platform while connecting emerging filmmakers with industry veterans.


The festival’s setting is no accident. Williamsburg is home to some of the country’s oldest African American historical sites, including First Baptist Church of Williamsburg, founded in 1776 by free and enslaved Black worshippers. Recent festival selections have explored that history directly: the documentary “History Half Told Is Untold,” which won Best Historical Feature at VBFF in 2024, traces the church’s remarkable story through archival research and interviews.


Beyond screenings, VBFF hosts panels, masterclasses, and discussions about everything from acting to distribution, turning a weekend of movies into a celebration of Black creativity. With past guests including Keith David, Daphne Maxwell Reid, Clifton Powell, and Tim Reid, the festival offers a rare chance to see nationally recognized artists alongside the next generation of filmmakers.


6. Yorktown Wine & Oyster Festival

Every October, the Yorktown Wine & Oyster Festival brings two local culinary traditions together on the banks of the York River: Virginia wines and Chesapeake oysters.


Long before European colonists arrived, Indigenous communities harvested oysters from the Chesapeake Bay. By the colonial era, oysters had become a staple of Virginia diets, and by the 19th century they had grown into one of the state’s most important industries. After decades of decline, restoration efforts and oyster farming have helped revive Virginia’s shellfish, with modern growers emphasizing the distinct flavors of different waterways.


The wine side of the festival reflects another Virginia tradition with deep roots. Early colonists experimented with grape growing soon after arriving in Jamestown, and today, Virginia’s vineyards produce everything from crisp viogniers to cabernet francs and sparkling wines. Nearby producers such as Williamsburg Winery and other Chesapeake Bay–area vineyards showcase how the state’s agricultural traditions continue to evolve.


Set against Yorktown’s historic waterfront, the festival offers a reminder that some of the region’s oldest traditions are still very much alive.


7. Yorktown Victory Weekend

Every October, Yorktown relives the moment when the American Revolution reached its dramatic conclusion. Yorktown Victory Weekend commemorates the 1781 siege that forced British General Charles Cornwallis to surrender, signaling the end of major fighting in the Revolutionary War.


Victory Weekend unfolds across one of the most significant preserved battlefields in the United States. Visitors can explore Revolutionary War encampments, watch artillery demonstrations, meet historical interpreters, and walk the same landscape where American and French troops built siege lines around the British position.


For visitors, Victory Weekend offers a chance to see history come alive: soldiers conducting drills, musicians performing 18th-century tunes, and interpreters telling the stories of the people who lived through the final chapter of the Revolution.


8. Grand Illumination

Each Saturday in December, Colonial Williamsburg transforms its Historic Area into a glowing recreation of an 18th-century holiday celebration, when candlelit windows, crackling cressets, music, and fireworks turned the colonial capital into a nighttime spectacle.


The tradition takes inspiration from colonial “illuminations”—public celebrations in which communities marked important occasions with candlelight, artillery fire, and fireworks. In the 18th century, these displays celebrated events ranging from military victories to the arrival of a new colonial governor. More recently, Colonial Williamsburg revived that spirit for holiday seasons.


During Grand Illumination evenings, visitors can wander streets lined with candlelit windows before gathering for musical performances and fireworks above some of Williamsburg’s most recognizable landmarks. The Governor’s Palace and the Capitol become dramatic backdrops for the finale, while the Historic Area remains decorated throughout the holiday season with wreaths, garlands, and other festive arrangements.


9. Christmas Market on Main

For one December weekend, Historic Yorktown becomes a festive gathering place filled with local artisans, seasonal foods, live music, and handcrafted gifts. Like the traditional Christmas markets of Europe, Yorktown’s market is built around the pleasures of slowing down: wandering between stalls, admiring handmade ornaments and artwork, warming up with a cup of hot cocoa or mulled wine, and sharing seasonal treats with friends and family.


The market is part of Yorktown’s larger holiday season, which combines the town’s maritime setting with winter traditions. After browsing local makers and sipping something warm, visitors can continue exploring the waterfront lights and nearby holiday events.


10. Lighted Boat Parade

In most holiday parades, the floats roll down a street. In Yorktown, they sail past on the water. On the first Saturday of December, boat owners along the York River decorate their vessels with thousands of lights for the Yorktown Lighted Boat Parade, turning the waterfront into a festive floating procession.


The parade typically features sailboats, fishing boats, and recreational vessels decked out for the season with glowing masts, illuminated hulls, wreaths, Christmas trees, and playful nautical decorations. Visitors gather along Riverwalk Landing to watch the boats drift past the historic waterfront.


Yorktown’s riverfront once served as a vital colonial port and later played a decisive role during the Revolutionary War. Today, these same waters are home to a much more festive kind of spectacle: a nighttime parade where the town’s maritime identity becomes part of its holiday celebration.


11. Busch Gardens Food & Wine Festival

From April through June, Williamsburg’s Busch Gardens trades its usual theme park fare for a culinary passport. The Food & Wine Festival spreads more than 135 international options across 17 themed locations throughout the park. The lineup ranges from Virginia specialties such as a Chesapeake-style crab cake sliders and jalapeño-cheddar hushpuppies to international dishes, including Ghanaian kelewele, Brazilian churrasco, Turkish döner kebabs, Polish pierogi, Hawaiian kālua pork sliders, and Puerto Rican mofongo and ceviche.


The festival also highlights Virginia producers, with beers from Williamsburg-area breweries like Alewerks Brewing Company and The Virginia Beer Company, and wines such as viognier from The Williamsburg Winery and chardonnay from Barboursville Vineyards. Specialty cocktails, international wines and beers, and exclusive tastings round out the offerings, turning a day of roller coasters into a progressive meal that winds through the park.
